item.title:
[karpathy]We'll be spending a lot more time trying to understand the outputs of language models. A few thoughts, tips & tricks:
Writing. Something I've had success with: Ask your LLM to explain something in ASD-STE100, it's a controlled language specification originally developed for aerospace maintenance documentation. LLMs well-versed in this language and it comes with heavy constraints on clean writing style that I often find a lot more readable. Sometimes I've tried to soften it a bit e.g. ask for "80% of the way to ASD-STE100" because the spec is quite stringent. But even better:
Diagrams / images. Instead of writing, ask your LLM to create a diagram. These can be a lot easier to process, parse, and understand. But even better:
Web pages. Ask for output "in HTML" to get a beautiful, interactive webpage. LLMs are getting really good at frontend and can create beautiful experiences, animations, etc. But even better:
Explainer videos. The output format I am most bullish on is fully custom / bespoke explainer videos generated on any arbitrary topic. Experiment with things like "Create a 3b1b style video explainer on X. Use my ElevenLabs API key for audio narration". (you'd need an API key for the latter or you can ask your LLM to find you decent free alternatives that use your local compute). This is actually starting to work!
In summary: - As LLMs get better, they will do more and more of the legwork autonomously, and a lot more of our work will rise up the abstractions into oversight and understanding. - Luckily, LLMs can help here too because as intelligence and code are increasingly abundant, you can ask for large, custom, discardable software artifacts (e.g. web apps, video explainers) that would have never made sense to create before. Push the boundaries here and you'll be surprised.

That is the signal.
States do this when they believe something is important enough that waiting for the market to sort itself out becomes strategically dangerous. Nuclear technology, space, semiconductors, energy, defense. Once the government creates a permanent coordinating apparatus around a technology, that technology has crossed from industry into state power.
The phrase “Super Intelligence Force” reveals the assumed end state. They are not organizing around chatbots or productivity software. They are organizing around the possibility that machine intelligence becomes one of the primary determinants of national power.
That means the race changes character.

So capability development becomes strategically compelled.
The strangest part is that governments are now beginning to build institutions for a form of intelligence that could eventually exceed the cognitive capability of the institutions governing it.
That is historically unusual.
Human institutions are preparing to administer something potentially more intelligent than the humans inside them.
If this architecture persists, October 2026 may eventually look like the period when AI stopped being treated primarily as technology and started being treated as a new component of sovereignty.

[YIsah16]What if you could use AI without doing the boring work yourself?
That question got me curious about @ActionModelAI
Because think about how we use AI today.
“Write this.”
“Research that.”
“Give me the steps.”
AI gives you the answer.
Then you close the chat, open five tabs, click through a website, copy information, fill a form and do the actual work yourself.
That gap is what caught my attention.
Action Model is building Large Action Models (LAMs) around a simple shift:
Don’t just tell AI what to do. Let it take action.
A LAM can see what’s happening on a screen, decide what needs to happen next, interact with the interface, check the result and continue through a workflow.
That’s where Actionist comes in, turning this capability into something that can handle practical, multi step tasks.
But the part I kept coming back to wasn't just the automation.
It was the community.
People can contribute real interactions that help train the system, while the ecosystem is designed to let contributors participate in the value they help create.
And that changes the question.
We’re used to AI companies building models and everyone else simply using them.
What happens when the people helping build the intelligence can have a stake in the ecosystem too?
That’s the experiment I’m watching.
AI has spent years learning how to talk to us.
The next leap may be teaching it how to act.
And when that happens, the biggest change might not be smarter answers.
It might be fewer things we have to do ourselves.

[TAsimovF]I think we finally got there, meet Ollie.
This started almost two years ago as an embodied AI + robotics project built around the preserved exterior of my old cat. Inside is a custom robotic frame with actuators, joint feedback, cameras, microphones, touch sensing, local edge compute and closed-loop motor control. The behavioral side came from years of old iPhone footage. I extracted pose, gait timing, head turns, ear movement, response delays, routines and behavioral patterns, then used that data to shape motion, memory and behavior. And thanks to @Grok because he became the main reasoning layer, connected to local vision, speaker recognition, spatial audio, persistent memory and the behavior controller. The motors are still handled by a separate local robotics stack.
The hardest part wasn’t making him intelligent. It was making him stop moving like a robot. Early versions were too smooth, too symmetrical and too responsive. Months went into tuning tiny things like ear-first orientation, uneven step timing, weight shifts, delayed reactions and sometimes no reaction at all.
He isn’t Ollie resurrected or uploaded consciousness. He’s a robotic system built around the preserved form and recorded behavioral data of one specific cat. I started calling him an Artificial Intelligence Cat. After the recent government shift toward “Super Intelligence” terminology, I figured the name should change too.
So this is Ollie. My Super Intelligence Cat.
Ill be posting more videos of him through out the day and week. I don't want to give away my precious work all at once.

[karpathy]Dusting off this tweet from April because this gap in shared understanding of LLM capability is *widening*. It's now less "two groups of people speaking past each other" and more a sharp funnel.
- Napkin math somewhere around 6B people (~75% of the population) have barely come in contact with LLMs at all. - Around 1-2B (~20%) are casual and infrequent users of free-tier ChatGPT-like products. This group sees derpy chatbots and treats them a bit like a better Google search, a writing aid, or etc. Maybe an agent tries to book you a flight. I have non-tech friends who (reasonably, imo) say they have not much use for it at all. Even many professionals outside of math&code are in this tier. For example, execs and many other functions spend a lot of their time talking to other people, so while they understand what is happening intellectually, it is still second-hand and a bit abstract. - Now we get to professional use of frontier-grade LLMs in math&code. Somewhere around 20M people (0.2%) see first-hand that large, complex projects that used to take them weeks/months can now be completed by agents with a prompt. Building apps, copying apps, translating apps, decompiling apps from binaries... This has all happened very quickly and recently - less than 1 year ago, I was writing code manually by hand, typing memorized computer code commands into a code editor character by character, occasionally pressing Tab to autocomplete a little chunk of code. - And finally we get to the ~5,000 people (~0.00006%) with access to frontier-grade systems internally. The external world has seen the preview. It looks like swarms of thousands of agents collaborating over weeks on software mega projects: minting zero days, running cyber attacks and defenses at machine speeds, discovering new science, advancing the frontier of mathematics. Things that would have taken top professionals in the industry years of work. Meanwhile, human review and comprehension are starting to fall behind. For example, people are still involved in the "archeology" of the OpenAI-HF incident from many months ago. Mathematicians may be poring over the 722 manuscripts on frontier mathematics for a while.
The funnel is driven by a combination of factors: 1. The impact scales with ambition, problem size, and horizon. A question with a paragraph answer barely stresses the system. You need a reservoir of big, difficult problems that you really care about. This aspect drives the consumer / professional dimension of the funnel. 2. The jaggedness of the system (which I have written about a lot separately). Capability peaks in domains that are digital, verifiable and economically valuable. This is because LLM capability emerges from reinforcement learning on verifiable rewards on a curated environment mixture driven by revenue potential. This aspect primarily drives the area (e.g. math&code) dimension of the funnel. 3. Access. Free-tier, paid-tier, internal.
So this is the weirdness of the moment. The general public has mostly not interacted with these systems. When they have, it looks like a derpy chatbot. The majority of professionals still see only a modest uplift. And a small sliver of professionals are experiencing the vertigo of the curve going vertical. And it is all happening at the same time.

[neal_k_patel]You already gave the LLM the answer. So why is it writing it out from scratch?
Introducing a new AI model architecture: Constrained Decoding Models (CDMs)
LLMs were built to write. Most production workloads just need an answer: fast, consistent, and affordable.
CDMs are purpose-built for 1 task each. They read your input once and skip the token-by-token generative loop that makes LLMs slow and expensive.
Not just a decision model, but a family of 3 CDMs live today:
• Classify: define your labels and get back a calibrated probability + reason for each. Used for routing, tagging, and intent detection. • Extract: describe the entities in natural language and get back well-formed JSON with confidence scores + citations. Used for web scraping, document processing, and PII redaction. • Summarize: pass in long text, images, or PDFs and get back a consistent summary under 1,000 tokens. Used for context compaction, metadata generation, and transcript digests.
Built for production:
• 1M tokens of multimodal (text + image) input, 31x larger than Jev • 77.2% on DecisionBench vs Jev's 72% • 200x faster, 467x cheaper than frontier LLM APIs • $0.05/M input tokens. Output is free (yes, even for summarize)
